Thus far, it has been explained how the practitioner of contemplation generally realizes the emptiness of the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), yet has not yet realized the emptiness of the nature of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
If it were not revealed, there would be no means for entry; if one does not enter, the non-conceptual wisdom—namely, the practice of entering—will ultimately fail to be accomplished.
For the sake of revelation, he further says this: "The unconditioned has no reality; its non-arising is like a flower in the sky."

In this context, the specific terminology used to establish the thesis refers to the aforementioned intention of distinguishing the ultimate reality (*tattva*), as should be understood from what precedes.
It is with respect to ultimate reality that "unconditioned emptiness" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) is established, and not with respect to the conventional, because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

It is designated as "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*); its meaning is that which is the opposite of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This consists of space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the nature of suchness (*tathatā*).

Among these, a portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) mentioned previously was first presented for the sake of facilitating entry [into reality], because the emptiness of the nature of space is easy to demonstrate.
It is only with respect to that which is empty and lacks any material obstruction that the world collectively establishes the designation "space.
By means of this gateway, one realizes the emptiness of the remaining unconditioned phenomena.
That which is known as space in this world is, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*), empty and devoid of substantiality;

this is called the thesis (*pakṣa*). This very established thesis—that space, from the perspective of ultimate reality, lacks substantiality—is called the reason (*hetu*), because both parties agree that it is unarisen, or because it is conventionally designated as an unarisen phenomenon (*anutpāda-dharma*).

Because a flower in the sky lacks substance and likewise does not arise, it is established as a similar example (*sapakṣa*). One should understand, as previously explained, that it is not stated that the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is excluded to establish it as a dissimilar property example (*asapakṣadṛṣṭānta*).
How is inference established herein?
It is said that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*), space is without substantiality because it does not arise.
That which does not arise is known by both the ignorant and the wise to be devoid of intrinsic nature, just like a flower in the sky.
Regarding this established reason that "it does not arise," to briefly state its characteristics, there are further reasons:
because it is not something produced, because it is not a producer, and because it is subject to neither destruction nor decay.
Such reasons as these are capable of negating the aforementioned emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); therefore, they may all appropriately serve as reasons.

It is like saying, "You must guard this ghee and not let crows approach it"; for the sake of ensuring that what is being guarded remains free from damage or defilement, one must likewise ward off cats, mice, and other such creatures.
The Vaibhāṣika masters all raise this objection:

"If the thesis you have established—that unconditioned phenomena lack substantial reality—is accepted as meaning they do not exist, then how could the meditative attainments of the sphere of infinite space and so forth exist, since they would have no object of perception?"

However, non-obstruction is the defining characteristic of space. If one were to establish an inference through skillful means (*upāya*), one might say: "The meditative attainment of the sphere of space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samāpatti*) truly possesses an object of cognition, or its object is truly existent, because it is a meditative attainment, or because it is the object of cognition of a meditative attainment."

Whether it be other meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) or their respective objects, since those other attainments and their objects are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are already established as empty of intrinsic nature; thus, there is no analogous example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

This has been an exposition of the characteristics of space from the perspective of ultimate truth; however, from the perspective of conventional truth, the space established therein is also not substantially existent, because it does not arise, just like a flower in the sky.
By this inference, that which you have established as substantially existent is not proven.

Furthermore, by means of the very reason I have stated, your claim that "it is because it is the object of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)" incurs the fault of a definitive contradiction (*viruddha-hetu*).
Therefore, the thesis I previously established is proven, as it is free from any obstacles or difficulties.
Members of our own school and other schools have stated:
"From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*), space is not real, because it does not arise."
By the logic of this statement, that which arises is necessarily real.
If one were to say that even that which arises lacks reality, then this reason would not be present in all similar instances (sapakṣa), and the nature of the reason would be unestablished.
This is an *arthāpatti* (implication by meaning); it is a fallacy of similarity that resembles the fallacy of non-establishment (*asiddha*).
This is a definitive statement: "All things that do not arise are without reality";
it is not a definitive statement: "All things that lack reality do not arise."
Even though it is produced through diligent and uninterrupted effort, it is accepted as a cause even if it does not pervade the similar class (*sapakṣa*); therefore, there is no fault here.
Others raise this objection:
"Space has an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for this is commonly known in the world; likewise, the lotus and other flowers also have an intrinsic nature, for they are perceived by the world."

"Although the two things—emptiness and flowers—are not mutually associated, it is not the case that they lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva); therefore, the analogy of 'empty flowers' fails to establish its point.
This objection is not valid.

This analogy of "empty flowers" is explained according to the sixth grammatical case (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) as "the flower of emptiness" (*śūnyasya puṣpam*); thus it is called "empty flowers. Since this [flower] does not exist, the analogy is not non-existent.

By this principle, practitioners of meditation should correctly realize and enter into the emptiness of the nature of space, and they should likewise realize and enter into the principle of the emptiness of the nature of the three types of unconditioned phenomena, such as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters, unable to tolerate the refutation of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), further raise this objection:

"The Buddha taught that analytical cessation is the antidote to the conditioned and is therefore called 'renunciation' (*niḥsaraṇa*); if you falsely deny its existence, you incur the fault of contradicting your own tenets.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:"
"It is said that 'the cessation of all feelings accompanied by joy and greed is called the quiescent, subtle, and wondrous state of nirvāṇa.
How can you say it does not exist?

Herein, because the Blessed One intends for those to be trained to diligently cultivate weary detachment toward conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and to accord with and rejoice in unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), he speaks of the existence of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), renunciation, and the quiescent, subtle, and wondrous state of nirvāṇa according to conventional truth."

Just as the Buddha taught that there are sentient beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*), so too did he teach that there is unconditioned nirvāṇa; since this existence is accepted, there is no fault of contradicting our own tenets.
However, it is with respect to ultimate reality (*tattva*) that [nirvāṇa as] analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is negated; therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Those who seek nirvāṇa as having an intrinsic nature (*bhāva-svabhāva*), I call them foolish followers of non-Buddhist teachers."
...and so on, as explained at length;
furthermore, it says:
"The Tathāgata does not perceive saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa."
"What is called 'nirvāṇa' is a designation established by the Tathāgata; herein, there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of nirvāṇa whatsoever.
This is explained at length.

Furthermore, there is no fault of slandering the Noble Truths, because it is from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) that one speaks of the ultimate non-arising of the suffering of craving, its transcendence, and the quiescent, subtle, and non-erroneous state of nirvāṇa. It is not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that the ultimate non-arising of the suffering of craving and its primordial cessation are designated as the Truth of Cessation.
Based on this sacred teaching and the reasoning therein set forth, it is said that there is no non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) from the perspective of ultimate reality;
thus, there is no such fault. Other proponents of incorrect reasoning raise this objection:
"The thesis you establish—that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack substantial reality—is untenable."
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist, that which is established is not established, nor is its basis established;

because a flower in the sky does not exist, the property of the subject (*dharmin*) is not established, and thus the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) all possess fallacies.
This objection is not valid.

By the power of conceptual designation (*saṃjñā-prajñapti*), one establishes "space" (*ākāśa*) based solely on the absence of any material object possessing resistance (*sapratigha*). Through the discernment of wisdom (*prajñā-vicaya*), one establishes "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) based solely on the non-arising of afflictions (*kleśa*). Due to the deficiency of various conditions (*pratyaya-vaikalya*), one establishes "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) based solely on the non-arising of all phenomena (*dharma*). And based solely on the absence of all that is grasped (*parikalpita*), one establishes "suchness" (*tathatā*).

Because the power of conceptual designation allows for the provisional establishment of space and so forth, their specific distinctions are not explicitly manifested. By the force of common consensus, one establishes a general property (*dharmin*); the exclusion of specific [unshared] attributes—which are not commonly known—is established as the thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*). That which is commonly understood, such as its non-arising and so forth, is established as the reason-property (*hetudharma*). Therefore, there is no fault in establishing either the thesis or the reason.

Although the "empty flowers" mentioned have no real entity, they possess the nature of being the "nature of the non-existence of entities" (dharmanairātmya) within the category of phenomena that do not arise; therefore, they are capable of establishing the thesis to be proven, and thus there is no fault of the subject (dharmin) being unestablished.
The Vaibhāṣika masters further state: This is also not the case;

analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is substantially existent because it is the object of the Path and because it opposes the afflictions; for such a thing could not exist if it were a non-substantial dharma.

This statement merely serves to exclude the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); for example, it is like excluding the real existence of space (*ākāśa*). Since this has already been thoroughly refuted previously, it should not be clung to again.

All the masters of the Sautrāntika school maintain that the postulation of space and so forth as being non-real constitutes the fault of establishing what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) through such inference (*anumāna*).

If this statement means that obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and so forth have non-existence as their essence, it does not establish what is already established, because their non-existence has already been demonstrated.

When the thesis states that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack substantial reality, these words primarily refute the attachment to substantial existence, while also incidentally refuting the attachment to substantial non-existence.
The teacher of the Tāmraparṇīya school further states:

"The color of the intervening spaces is called space; since our school establishes it as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), your attempt to negate it commits the fallacy of refuting what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)."
Since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of conditioned phenomena has already been refuted as before, this [position] is likewise untenable.
The tenets held by the Vaibhāṣikas and the Vātsīputrīyas are largely identical; therefore, they should be refuted in the same manner as those [Vaibhāṣikas].
The masters of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (*Saṃprayuktaka-śāstra*) have stated:

"Beyond the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no further ultimate truth; suchness (*tathatā*) itself is the ultimate truth of all phenomena. Therefore, it is in terms of the ultimate truth that one speaks of the emptiness of suchness. This statement accords with reason. However, to say that suchness is not substantially existent does not accord with reason. Why is this?
It is logically consistent that supramundane non-conceptual wisdom and the subsequently attained pure mundane wisdom take unconditioned phenomena as their objects; however, it is truly not logical.

Just as it is said that it is not logically consistent for mundane wisdom to take unconditioned phenomena as its object, so too is it not logically consistent for this [subsequently attained] wisdom to take conditioned phenomena as its object.
It is not reasonable to maintain that *tathatā* (suchness) exists as a real entity, because its existence as a real entity is difficult to establish.

The wisdom that takes *tathatā* as its object is not truly supramundane non-conceptual wisdom, because it possesses an objective referent and is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like mundane wisdom that takes objects.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Mañjuśrī!
What does the wisdom-eye see?"
He replied:
"The eye of wisdom sees nothing at all.
It is further said:
"What is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)? He replied:
"In this, even wisdom does not operate, let alone names."
Furthermore, it is said:
"O Brahmin! The awakening of the Tathāgata is not something that can be directly realized."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"Mañjuśrī, how does one see the truths?"
He replied: "In this state, there is no dharma that can be seen or recollected.
According to these various sūtras, one should not admit that this non-conceptual wisdom is capable of direct realization (*abhisamaya*) or that it takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
Furthermore, that suchness is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Moreover, regarding your statement that "there is no further ultimate reality upon the ultimate reality," if one says something is "empty" because that [object] is absent from this [locus], then since there is no cloth or silk upon other pieces of cloth or silk, even shepherds and others would commonly understand this; they too should be called seers of the truth.

Furthermore, such emptiness is taught as an antidote to various wrong views; since no such wrong views have ever existed regarding a further ultimate truth upon the ultimate truth, there would be no need to negate them by teaching such emptiness.
Furthermore, that *tathatā* (suchness) does not possess a nature of real existence, as this would contradict the principles of inference (*anumāna*) explained previously.

As it is said: "The Tathāgata perceives neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; he has correctly realized that the afflictions arising from inversion do not exist, and that their fundamental nature is ultimately without birth and is the very essence of self-nature. Thus, one correctly knows that the fundamental nature is ultimate; it is not a case of correct knowledge, nor is it incorrect knowledge.

Based on this sacred teaching, one should know that *tathatā* (suchness) is simply the eternal cessation of all conceptual construction; it is neither a real entity nor something apart from non-existence.

The true nature of reality (*dharmatā-tathatā*) has the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) as its characteristic and constitutes the accomplishment of the *dharmakāya*. By attaining the path of direct antidote that contemplates emptiness, all seeds of conceptual construction and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), along with the seeds of conceptualization within the *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness) which serves as their support, are forever severed without remainder. Because the causes and conditions no longer exist, they never arise again; being by nature unarisen and by nature eternally abiding, this is called the *dharmakāya* as the transformed basis of the Tathāgata.
As stated in a sutra:
"Mañjuśrī! To speak of the Tathāgata is to speak of the phrase that is ultimately and fundamentally unborn."
"The dharmas that are eternally unarisen are called the Tathāgata," and so forth,
as explained at length.

If one were to say that although *tathatā* (suchness) is beyond verbal expression, it exists substantially, this would merely be the self (*ātman*) of the non-Buddhists being designated by the different names and concepts of "suchness."

Just as that *tathatā* (suchness), although it is substantially existent, cannot be established through conceptual constructions such as "existence" or "non-existence" from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), so too am I.

They also maintain that although the self is substantially existent, all-pervading, and eternal, it is free from conceptual construction as the agent and the experiencer; because it is not within the range of linguistic expression, and because it is not an object of discursive cognition (*vikalpa-buddhi*), it is said to be "free from conceptual construction."
In that teaching, it is said that because verbal expression does not apply and the mind and consciousness do not realize it, it is called the "Self" (ātman).

While the characteristics of the Self are thus, it further states that liberation is attained by relying on the wisdom that takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its object, and not by relying on the wisdom that takes the Self as its object.
What is the distinction here?
Since there is no verbal expression that possesses a real nature, these are merely partisan assertions made by those who hold such views.
Therefore, I cannot accept such a semblance of true thusness as being either truly existent or non-existent.

Let us cease this extensive debate, for those who find the meaning of such voluminous texts daunting would find it difficult to uphold them; thus, having already entered the true nectar, we have analyzed this in detail.
Furthermore, there are those of similar standing who follow inferior vehicles and speak as follows:

"The twelve bases (*āyatana*) encompassing both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) must certainly possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is because one contemplates the Four Noble Truths through the sixteen noble aspects (*āryākāra*), such as suffering and so forth, and by diligently practicing the two paths of seeing and cultivation, one is able to extinguish the blazing fires of all afflictions (*kleśa*) included within the three realms that are to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation, and cause the manifold sufferings of the three realms to cease."
If the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena were not revealed, who would be able to abandon such faults,
and who again would be able to cultivate such virtues?
Although there are differences among the three vehicles regarding their accumulations, faculties, and inclinations, there should be no difference in the noble path of direct realization.
I accept all of this as true; however, for the purpose of severing the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one relies on the conventional truth regarding the distinctions of those paths.

If one were to exclude the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), it would be impossible to permanently sever the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); consequently, the Great Teacher [the Buddha] would only have attained partial liberation.
Is it not the case that you do not say there is no difference between liberation and liberation?
Indeed, such a statement exists; it is said thus because they are all equally liberated from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but this does not apply to every respect.
For example, although the space within a pore and the great void are identical in their emptiness, they are not without distinction.
If this were not so, one would be unable to manifest the functional efficacy of superior fruits, such as the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and what is realized would not be truly ultimate.
Let us set aside this digression and return to the primary argument.

A practitioner of meditation who has already realized the emptiness of space and other categories as conceived by their own school must likewise realize the emptiness of those categories as conceived by other schools, such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), the Lord (*īśvara*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), and the life-force (*jīva*).
In this regard, the proponents of the theory of the self-nature person (svabhāva-puruṣa-vādin) raise this objection:
"In our school, all things in the three realms are transformations resembling flowers in the sky; it is not that flowers in the sky do not exist."
Because that [subject] exists, the concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is unestablished, as it contradicts the thesis (*sādhya*).
Now one should interrogate:
when you say that all things in the three realms are transformations resembling flowers in the sky, are these three realms themselves flowers in the sky?
Is it not like a flower in the sky?
If you say that the three realms are all like flowers in the sky, this contradicts your own tenet as well as common knowledge, and is therefore unreasonable.
If you say that the three realms are not like flowers in the sky, then there would be no similar example to establish your point, and you would lose your original position.
If you say it is not lost, then a flower in the sky has no sound.

As for your claim that the triple world possesses intrinsic nature, you should first examine this carefully: do you mean that I am using "a flower in the sky" as a similar instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) because it is non-existent?
Is the "flower in the sky" (ākāśapuṣpa) being presented as the similar example (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*)?

If you claim that I am stating the non-existence of the flower in the sky as the similar example, this is a poor examination, because I have indeed stated the flower in the sky as the similar example.

If the flower in the sky is stated as the similar example, it is not part of the three realms (*traidhātuka*); therefore, one should not say that because the three realms exist, it too exists. This statement merely reveals the meagerness of your own intelligence.

Furthermore, regarding negative expressions (*paryudāsa*), the act of negation is primary; once the object of negation has been excluded, the function [of the expression] is exhausted, and it lacks the capacity to further express the specific distinctions of that which was negated.
Such objections have already been fully explained above; therefore, they are not what the minds of the wise accept.
The Sāṃkhya teachers further state:

"Although we cannot directly establish the existence of the Supreme Puruṣa through direct perception, we can nonetheless establish its substantial reality through the method of common consensus regarding the collection of transformations. That is to say, all manifest phenomena have 'Being' (sattā) as their cause, because they possess a common genus;
and whatever possesses a common genus is seen to have 'Being' as its cause, just as in the case of pieces of sandalwood and the like."
Since manifest phenomena (vyakta) possess a common genus, they have "existence" (sattā) as their cause; likewise, these manifest phenomena have a recipient, because they are objects of enjoyment.
All things that are enjoyed are seen to have a recipient, just as in the case of the food and drink enjoyed by a Brahmin.

Since manifest phenomena (*vyakta*) are objects of experience, there must be an experiencer; thus, the inference previously stated is subverted by a counter-inference (*pratikūla-pramāṇa*). This is from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).

If one were to establish the existence of a nature (*svabhāva*) in all manifest phenomena based on their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) without distinguishing their specific differences, one would merely be proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*).

If one posits pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth as the cause of manifest phenomena, there would be no similar example (*sapakṣa*), and the reason (*hetu*) would also be unestablished, because the categories of pleasure and so forth are not commonly accepted [as such].

If one seeks to establish the statement regarding the cause through inference (*anumāna*), then the four aggregates (*skandha*) are all of the nature of suffering, pleasure, and delusion, because they possess the nature of being aggregates.
As for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the delusion (*moha*) mentioned here is not subsumed within that aggregate; thus, the supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished.

Furthermore, since your "person" (*pudgala*) possesses a manifold nature, is omnipresent, and has the sense of being a collection, it carries the very meaning of an "aggregate" (*skandha*); therefore, the reason regarding this person is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, since your respective positions—such as pleasure and so forth—are individually incapable of establishing a thesis because they possess the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished.

If, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one were to claim that there exists a real piece of sandalwood with "existence" as its reason, it would not be established by common consensus; thus, the concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished.

Furthermore, from a conventional perspective, if one establishes that among manifest phenomena there is a "receiver" based on their general characteristics, then to fail to distinguish their specific differences is to establish what is already established, for the existence of a receiver is commonly known in the world.

If one were to establish that the manifest entity possesses a real experiencer who is permanent, omnipresent, and has volition (*cetanā*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be unestablished; for such a definition of its essential characteristics is not commonly accepted even by the Brahmins.

If one proceeds from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is not established, because the existence of the eater and the food as real entities (*dravyasat*) is not commonly accepted.
Regarding the aforementioned inference (*anumāna*), there is no opposing capacity (*prati-vidhātṛ*) capable of subverting it.
The Vaiśeṣika masters further state:

The various characteristics such as inhalation and exhalation, closing and opening the eyes, causing the movement of the mind, and the transformation of the sense faculties must necessarily have corresponding characterized objects (lakṣya), because they are characteristics (lakṣaṇa), just like seeing smoke and so forth.

This is from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). If one were to establish those various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as having a determinate characterized object (*lakṣya*) by means of their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), then without distinguishing their specific differences, one would merely be establishing what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for it is conventionally and universally known that the self (*ātman*) is not non-existent.

If one posits that the self (*ātman*), characterized by those attributes, is permanent, omnipresent, and the substratum of pleasure and so forth, then there would be no similar example (*sapakṣa*), as this would contradict what is being established.
Even from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is likewise the fault of the example being unestablished (*asiddha*).
By this same reasoning, space, direction, time, and so forth should also be refuted.
The Vaiśeṣikas further raise this objection:
"In establishing the reason for emptiness—that atoms and the mind are unconditioned because they do not arise—your own reason is not established."

If it is argued that these two are included within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and thus establish the reason for emptiness because they are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), then this reason would not be established for others, and one would consequently only partially realize emptiness.
If one were to concede that the mind and atoms are also unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in the conventional sense, then this objection would hold.
However, the mind as it is here proposed is not unconditioned, because it is a cause for the arising of cognition, just like form (*rūpa*) and other such phenomena.
Because these phrases share the same or different meanings, and because they are the causes for the arising of mindfulness, other such causes should be explained accordingly.
Furthermore, atoms are not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because they are capable of being causes, just like threads and the like.
In this same manner, other reasons such as conjunction, disjunction, number, and identity or difference should be stated as appropriate.
Alternatively, a gross object composed of two atoms cannot have permanence as its cause, because it is something produced, just like a jar and so forth.
Likewise, because the rest are produced, because they are subject to destruction, and because they possess causes—these reasons should be stated as appropriate.
By this principle, the mind and atoms, which others falsely imagine to exist, are both empty of intrinsic nature; therefore, there is no fault as has been alleged.

As explained above, having refuted through various principles the categories (*padārtha*) of the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools, the categories maintained by the Nirgrantha and other systems should likewise be established as empty according to their respective cases.

Having thus dispelled all objections and difficulties, the practitioner of meditation, by means of the power of correct inference, realizes that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) entities asserted by both their own and others' schools are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnya).

Although one has entered into the emptiness of intrinsic nature through the power of the stages of wisdom consisting of hearing, because one lacks the power of superior cultivation, one is unable to permanently sever the obstacles that ought to be eliminated; therefore, one again applies oneself with diligence to practicing the power of superior cultivation.

If, within this context, any one of these characteristics of the conditioned or the unconditioned—whether intermittent or continuous—should manifest again, one should then contemplate its emptiness of intrinsic nature according to reason. By dispelling those characteristics so that they no longer appear, one enters into the realization of all phenomena, for they are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Its nature is fundamentally empty; because its nature is empty, its characteristics do not become substantial, which is signlessness (*animitta*).
Because it is signless, there is nothing to be sought or desired, which is wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Because it is free from the defilement of marks, it constitutes remoteness; furthermore, because it is free from intrinsic nature, the afflictions directed toward it never arise, and thus it constitutes tranquility.
Because its self-nature is without arising, it constitutes non-arising; because there is no arising, there is neither impermanence, nor suffering, nor non-self.

Furthermore, because there is no arising, there are no marks; and because there are no marks, one can, through the practice of the single mark of no-mark, contemplate all phenomena and awaken to their non-duality.
By means of this mode of practice, one diligently cultivates superior cultivation; because the power of such superior cultivation increases, coarse signs are eliminated so that they no longer appear.

Through this, there is a state of non-practice regarding signs—namely, the grasping at conditioned and unconditioned signs—just as one with cataracts, once freed from coarse visual opacities, attains clarity of vision and no longer sees the various signs previously grasped.

Although one has already attained non-abiding within this state, because the conceptualization of emptiness and so forth still manifests, the mind of effortful application continues to persist; thus, one has not yet attained immovability—the clear realization that the manifestation of conceptualizations such as emptiness obstructs supramundane non-conceptual wisdom.
Desiring to abandon [these misconceptions], one applies courageous and correct diligence, observing thus:

from the perspective of ultimate truth, even conceptualizations such as "emptiness" regarding the object of emptiness are not truly existent, because they arise dependently, just like illusions and the like.

By practicing with such diligence, one is further able to eliminate conceptual discriminations regarding emptiness and so forth; because those are eliminated, one remains far removed from the two extremes of emptiness and non-emptiness, and no longer examines phenomena through the mental aspects of emptiness and the like.

As it is said, when the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is correctly practiced, one does not regard form as permanent nor as impermanent; one does not regard it as pleasant nor as painful; one does not regard it as self nor as non-self; one does not regard it as tranquil nor as non-tranquil; one does not regard it as empty nor as non-empty; one does not regard it as having marks nor as being markless; one does not regard it as having aspirations nor as being aspirationless; and one does not regard it as detached nor as non-detached.

In this same way, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; all forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena; all eyes, ears, noses, tongues, bodies, and minds; the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; the applications of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path; the meditative concentrations, formless attainments, meditative absorptions, and supernormal powers; the ten powers, fearlessnesses, analytical knowledges, unique qualities of a Buddha, various samādhis, doors of dhāraṇī, and omniscience—one does not view them as permanent, nor as impermanent, and so forth, as explained at length.

Being thus able to remain far removed from these two extremes, one is then able to cultivate the sublime practice that abides in the middle way; this principle of abiding in the middle, free from the two extremes, is established by the two kinds of inference explained above.

Because the categories of conditioned and unconditioned form do not exist, it is called "formless" (*arūpa*). Due to this absence of form, there are also no conceptual distinctions such as existence and so forth; thus, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be characterized or indicated.
Since that is so, this is likewise; therefore, it is called "non-indication.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, both the supported and the supporter are not established; because there is no abiding or maintaining, it is called "non-abiding."

Whether it be the characteristic of the conditioned or the unconditioned, whether it be that which is discriminated or not discriminated, or that which discriminates or does not discriminate—since the wisdom of awakening does not function with respect to such characteristics as these, it is called "non-manifestation."
Because all consciousnesses regarding signs and signlessness are entirely non-arising, it is called "without discernment" (*avijñapti*).
Because it is formless, lacks substantiality, and is devoid of spatial dimensions or characteristics, it is called "without characteristics" (*animitta*).
As the Blessed One told Kāśyapa:
"Permanence is one extreme; impermanence is the second.

Between these two, there is no form, no demonstration, no abiding, no manifestation, no object of discernment, and no sign. This is called the sublime practice of the middle way, which observes the nature of all phenomena as they truly are."
The full exposition continues up to: "Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are one extreme, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are the second," and so forth.
Furthermore, as the Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Luminosity (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are both non-dual and without distinction; herein, correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is what is called the sublime practice of the middle way."

Being thus able to remain far removed from these two extremes, one also understands that even the conceptualization of a "non-dual thought" arising upon abiding in the perception of non-duality acts as an obstacle to the supramundane, non-conceptual wisdom that dwells in tranquility. By means of the causes as previously explained, one is swiftly and permanently able to sever it; because of that permanent severance, such and such conceptualizations no longer exist, and both verbal and mental expressions come to rest. One realizes the immovable, the unmanifest, and the signless, becoming free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One enters into the realization of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) within its objective sphere without wavering, and the sublime wisdom of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) abides in continuous succession.

Although one diligently cultivates the non-erroneous contemplation of emptiness, one ultimately does not realize emptiness as a fixed attainment; this is called the meditative concentration of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-dhyāna*).
As the Blessed One said:
"Though one practices meditative concentration, one does not practice meditative concentration by relying on form."
In this way, one cultivates meditative concentration without relying on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one cultivates meditative concentration without relying on the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
one cultivates meditative concentration without relying on forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena; and one does not dwell in conceptualization regarding the body.
Yet they cultivate meditative concentration; they cultivate meditative concentration without relying on dwelling in mental discrimination,
they cultivate meditative concentration without relying on earth, water, fire, or wind, they cultivate meditative concentration without relying on space,
the sun, the moon, or the constellations, and they cultivate meditative concentration without relying on Śakra, Brahmā, or the lords of the world.
He cultivates meditative concentration (dhyāna) without relying on the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
he cultivates meditative concentration without relying on this world or other worlds; he cultivates meditative concentration by abiding in the immovable realization that is neither high nor low;
and he cultivates meditative concentration without relying on the view of a self (ātman-dṛṣṭi).

In this way, one practices dhyāna without relying on views of a sentient being, a life-principle, a nourisher, a person, an individual, or a mind-born being, nor a manava; one practices dhyāna without relying on views of annihilation or permanence, existence or non-existence, or the view of existence; one practices dhyāna not for the sake of the exhaustion of outflows, not for the sake of entering the state of rightness and departure from birth, not for the sake of realizing the fruits [of the path], and not for the sake of ultimate non-action.

"Although one practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) for the sake of cultivating the non-erroneous contemplation of emptiness, one nevertheless practices meditative concentration without realizing emptiness as a direct experience.
Those who follow the *Saṃprayukta* school maintain a fixed position, asserting:
"The complete distancing from all conceptualizations of the grasped and the grasper is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)."

One then gives rise to a firm conviction toward this and practices with diligent application. Regarding this, others who examine it correctly state: although such wisdom arises without the aforementioned conceptualizations, because it arises following the marks of the signless object (*animitta-viṣaya*), because it is pursued by innate conceptualization (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), and because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is like other types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) involving conceptual cognition; thus, it does not constitute supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*lokottara-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Furthermore, because that which they conceive—the ultimate reality (*tathatā*) free from characteristics and beyond expression—is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), it does not constitute the ultimate in the same way that other objects of cognition do not; for this very reason, neither [of these two] is supreme.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is meant here by 'ultimate truth' (paramārtha-satya)?
It is that wherein even wisdom does not operate."
Furthermore, it is as if one were to ask:
"Mañjuśrī! Regarding what is called the 'eye of wisdom,' what should it observe?"
He replied:
"If there were even the slightest thing observed, it would not be the eye of wisdom.

Because this eye of wisdom is free from conceptual discrimination, it does not observe the conditioned, nor can it observe the unconditioned, for all unconditioned phenomena are not within the sphere of activity of this eye of wisdom."
By virtue of this reasoning and scriptural authority, one should also abandon that fixed attachment to this [view].

Furthermore, upon careful examination, it is said that even such supramundane non-conceptual wisdom does not exist as a real entity from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), because it arises dependently, just like a magical illusion.
Regarding any obstacles, difficulties, or faults that may exist, one should observe them correctly according to reason and eliminate them.

If a cognition is able to sever such fixed attachments, then because this [cognition] likewise possesses faults just like those [attachments], one should no longer apply diligent effort to analyze or explain it further.

Once such attachments have been eliminated, there is no longer any conceptual engagement (*abhisamskāra*) even toward the nature of the signless object of knowledge; because the necessary conditions are lacking, no further cognition arises. Due to this absence of conceptual engagement, it is called "true conceptual engagement" (*bhūta-abhisamskāra*).
As the World-Honored One said:
"What is called 'true practice and understanding'?
It means that regarding all phenomena there is no practice or understanding at all; this is what is called true practice and understanding."
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"The awakening of the Tathāgata is entirely without direct realization (abhisamaya).
And as it is asked:
“Mañjuśrī! What do those who have realized the truths see?
He replied:
“There is not even the slightest dharma that can be seen. Why is this?
For whatever is seen is entirely false and illusory; only when there is nothing seen is it called ‘seeing the Truth.’”
Furthermore, as it is asked:
"How should one diligently cultivate clear realization (abhisamaya)?
The answer is:
"If one knows that there is not even the slightest dharma to be conceptualized or discriminated, one should thus diligently cultivate clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
He asked again:
"How does one already realize clear realization?"
He replied,
"If one can contemplate that all phenomena are of an equal nature.
He asked again:
"Is there anyone who can see the equality of all phenomena?
He replied,
"There is no one who can see equality."
If there were anything seen, it would constitute an unequal view.

True practice, understanding, the vision of the truths, and clear realization all have the same meaning; at that time, when the practitioner of meditation does not engage in mind, mentation, consciousness, or cognition, it is called right practice and non-conceptual wisdom.
If one can thus practice non-practice, one will receive the true prediction of enlightenment from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"World-Honored One!..."
How does a bodhisattva practice so as to receive the true prophecy of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
“Brahmin! If at this time a bodhisattva does not practice arising and does not practice cessation; does not practice the wholesome and does not practice the unwholesome;
does not practice the mundane and does not practice the supramundane; does not practice that which is with outflows and does not practice that which is without outflows...”
It does not proceed with outflows; it does not proceed with the guilty nor with the blameless; it does not proceed with the conditioned nor with the unconditioned;
it does not proceed with the associated nor with the dissociated; it does not proceed with cessation nor with non-cessation;
it does not proceed with saṃsāra nor with nirvāṇa; it does not proceed with seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, or cognizing; it does not proceed with giving.
Furthermore, they abandon and fail to practice ethical discipline and restraint; they do not practice patience, do not practice diligence,
do not practice meditative concentration, do not practice samādhi, do not practice wisdom,
do not practice understanding, do not practice knowledge, and do not practice realization.

When a bodhisattva practices in this way—practicing without anything to practice—they receive from the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas the true prophecy regarding their unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Such practice of wisdom is called noble silence.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"To correctly reveal, as taught by the Buddha, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is called teaching the Dharma."
Furthermore, although one personally realizes this Dharma with the body, one does not observe a phenomenon apart from the body, nor does one observe a body apart from phenomena.

Observing in this way means observing neither duality nor non-duality. When observing thus, one does not follow the perceptions of the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*); because one does not engage in such observation, it is called "noble silence."

When one thus scrutinizes through both reasoning and scripture, the intrinsic nature of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is found to lack any causal agency; this applies whether it be the mind or wisdom, and whether it be the objective sphere of conceptualization or non-conceptualization.
Having known this, the sunlight of clear wisdom can dispel all the darkness of ignorance.
When the objects of the mind and wisdom appear, the wise do not grasp them;
their practice of wisdom is non-conceptual, acting without anything to act upon.
In this context, it is called "mind" (*citta*) because it either accumulates the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) or is itself accumulated by those seeds;
it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*) because it can maintain superior qualities or, through their maintenance, prevents them from dispersing.
That which is traversed by mind and wisdom is called the object of mind and wisdom; that which is traversed by the objects of the stages is called their differentiation.
The objects of the mind are all the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned, while the objects of wisdom are the emptiness of all that is conditioned and unconditioned.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"The wisdom that discerns the signless never turns back.
Here, "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) means appearing; it refers to the sense that the nature and characteristics of the objects traversed by mind and wisdom appear as if they were real.
Whatever categories of the elements such as earth, etc., whether taken collectively or individually;

likewise, whatever categories of the eye, etc., and of visible forms, etc., whether taken collectively or individually; likewise, whatever categories of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, whether taken collectively or individually;
likewise, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power...

The bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), the perfections (*pāramitā*),
all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the ten powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*),

all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), the gateways of dhāraṇī (*dhāraṇīmukha*), and the paths of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the arhat.
As for the fruit, whether categorized generally or specifically— ranging extensively up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)—
one is called a "knower" because one is able to correctly understand all phenomena as being free from error.
"By means of" refers to explaining the causal conditions for the characteristic of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
"Not grasping" means being without attachment and without views; it is the sense that awakened wisdom (*buddhi*) does not engage in conceptual construction (*parikalpa*).
By means of the cause of non-grasping, what is realized?
The practice of wisdom proceeds by way of non-discrimination and non-activity; this wisdom is precisely non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Although it is forever free from all conceptualization, its awakened insight increases and is conventionally designated as "gnosis."

Because there arises no characteristic from an object-sphere that is without image, without mark, and beyond words, and because even the conceptualization of intrinsic nature does not exist, it is called "non-conceptual.
Although there is no one who abides [in it], it is provisionally established by way of different states, just as one speaks of "the extinction of a lamp" or "the extinction of an Arhat."
When awakened wisdom increases, based on conventional discourse, this continuity is termed "non-conceptual.
Just as analytical knowledge is termed "conceptual," here the intended meaning is that when wisdom takes the non-arising of phenomena as its mode of activity, it is called "activity."

Because all aspects of the dharmatā of oneself and others are not seen through the activity of this wisdom, it is not called "able to see"; rather, that which is not able to see is designated as "true seeing."

Because it is that which is realized, it is not the case that what is not seen is made into the appearance of being seen—whether through conceptualization or non-conceptualization—so that true vision is established.
If True Suchness were of the nature of an object seen, it should not be described as being of a nature that is not visible.
Although the view of equality based on conventional truth is called the "true view," one should not cling to this as being the true view while regarding the view of inequality as such.
All that is visible is not ultimately real because it serves as a cause for the arising of conceptual understanding, just like water in a mirage; thus, all that is visible is not ultimately real.
If suchness were of a nature that could be seen, then the grasping of visible characteristics would not constitute true seeing;
yet if it is not visible, one should not say that suchness is realized through seeing.
If that which is seen is not the object of seeing, how can it be called "equality"?
Furthermore, since wisdom is conditioned and true suchness is unconditioned, their natures are unequal; if one were to see them as such, it would constitute an unequal view.
Furthermore, the nature of all phenomena is such that none are capable of seeing; seeing itself must likewise be so, for both share the same intrinsic nature of non-arising.
Thus, while not seeing, it is conventionally designated as "seeing," and this is not an inequality.
Furthermore, when one realizes all phenomena in a single kṣaṇa as being entirely without actualization (abhisamaya), this is called true actualization.

One should not raise the objection that because it would involve reflecting back upon its own essence, such an establishment would be difficult to prove, and thus cognition would fail to realize the true nature of cognition itself.
Since both types are not of a nature that can be seen as objects and are without distinction, they are realized simultaneously.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the wisdom that appears as an object is by its very nature unarisen; therefore, there is neither clear realization (*abhisamaya*) nor any attainment.
As stated in a sutra:
"You should not, by means of direct realization or attainment, perceive the essence of the Tathāgata as unconditioned, for it transcends all that falls within the range of the eye."
Thus it is, O brahmin!
When the Tathāgata sat peacefully upon the seat of enlightenment, he realized that all phenomena are unattainable, and he forever severed all afflictions arising from false and inverted views.
All such sūtras are consistent with this. Let us now set aside these incidental discussions and proceed to analyze the primary treatise.

To "travel" is called "practice" (*caryā*); because there is no traveling, it is called "no-practice" (*acaryā*). This is the realization of non-practice, which signifies the absence of origination and is non-conceptual wisdom. Because one practices by means of the characteristic of non-practice, that which is "no-practice" is itself designated as "practice."
This is a brief explanation, as was previously established regarding the fruit of right exertion.

For the practitioner of meditation who thus practices wisdom without conceptualization, they practice while not practicing; their practice is itself non-practice. They remain far removed from all objective referents and mental engagements (*manasikāra*), abiding nowhere among any phenomena, like empty space. Having abandoned all pervasive conceptual constructions (*parikalpita-vikalpa*), they are tranquil and serene as if having entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). They contemplate the nature of all phenomena and the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas—ineffable and beyond discernment, non-dual, without concealment, signless, and invisible; it cannot be expressed, being without birth or cessation, without arising or ending; tranquil and serene, without differentiation, signless and shadowless, free from all defilements, transcending all cognition, language, spheres of experience, and paths.
Although one observes in this way, there is nothing seen; seeing without seeing, seeing is itself non-seeing.

Because it is embraced by such wondrous vision, one is able to correctly increase an immeasurable mass of merit and evoke the fruit of boundless, subtle bliss. Being of a pure, single flavor, it can extinguish the suffering of others, benefiting all beings according to their rightful aspirations, like the king of medicinal trees.
Thus, correctly contemplating the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata by not perceiving the marks of existence or non-existence in any phenomena is called right view.
Bringing to rest all pervasive conceptualization and discrimination is called right intention.
Because one realizes that all phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), such that all verbal expressions are completely stilled, this is called Right Speech (*samyag-vāc*).
Because all phenomena are not something produced, one does not create the causes thereof—namely, the karmas of body, speech, and mind—this is called Right Action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Because all phenomena are of a nature that neither increases nor decreases, such that all increase and decrease never arise, this is called right livelihood.
Because all phenomena are without initiation and without volitional construction, the courageous application of skillful means is called right effort.
Because one ultimately does not realize the nature of existence or non-existence regarding all phenomena, being without recollection and without conceptualization, this is called right mindfulness.
Because one does not grasp at any phenomena in any way and has no basis for dwelling, this is called right concentration.
Thus, through correct contemplation, one is able to cultivate this Eightfold Noble Path; the meaning of this is explained extensively throughout various sections of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*.

Such correct contemplation not only enables the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path, but can also bring to perfection the six perfections (*pāramitā*) as briefly described, even though no deliberate application (*prayoga*) is involved.
What is its meaning?
It refers to being able to relinquish all types of signs and being able to relinquish all afflictions; this is called the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Being able to still all mental engagements with objects of observation and cultivating non-apprehension; this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
To be unable to tolerate any objects of perception is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
to be without grasping or abandoning, and to be free from all conditioned activities, is called the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
for all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) to cease to manifest and to be entirely without activity is called the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
To not give rise to conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena and to remain far removed from dualistic characteristics is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This meaning is explained extensively in various places, such as the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra* and other scriptures.

Such sublime abidings have immeasurable gateways, which the World-Honored One has extensively expounded in countless sūtras; they possess great significance and benefit, providing vast assistance and profit. All who possess wisdom should understand them as they truly are and, free from all negligence, should diligently practice and study them.
